common_name: Kim's Knee High Echinacea (Classic Dwarf Reflexed-Petal Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Kim's Knee High is a classic dwarf coneflower cultivar, standing about knee-high (18-24 inches) rather than the taller 3-4 feet of the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Kim's Knee High is a long-popular dwarf coneflower cultivar bearing rich rose-pink, downward-reflexed petals around a spiny orange-brown cone, on a compact, sturdy plant that stays well below the height of the wild species without staking. Its manageable size fits smaller borders and front-of-bed plantings while still delivering the summer-long bloom and outstanding drought tolerance the genus is known for, along with strong appeal to butterflies, bees, and, once seed heads form, goldfinches. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering, or leave the last flush of seed heads standing into fall and winter as a food source for birds. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Sombrero Echinacea Series (Compact Branching Coneflower Series)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Sombrero is a coneflower breeding series bred for compact size, improved branching, heavy bloom, and a wide range of flower colors.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. The Sombrero series is a modern coneflower breeding line selected for compact, well-branched plants that produce an unusually heavy volume of flowers over a long summer-to-fall bloom season, available in a wide range of colors from classic purple-pink through red, orange, and yellow shades not found in the wild species. Its improved branching habit means more flowers per plant without staking, and like other coneflowers it is highly drought-tolerant once established and attracts butterflies, bees, and seed-eating birds. Deadhead to prolong bloom, or leave a final flush of seed heads standing for winter interest and bird forage. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Ruby Star Echinacea (Rosy-Red Flat-Petaled German Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Ruby Star (Rubinstern), an older German-bred coneflower cultivar, is valued for its rosy-red petals held nearly flat rather than drooping downward.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Ruby Star, also sold under its original German name Rubinstern, is a well-established coneflower cultivar bred for rich, rosy-red petals held nearly horizontal around the coppery-orange cone, rather than sweeping sharply downward as in the wild species, giving each flower a fuller, more substantial look. Sturdy, well-branched stems hold up well through summer storms without staking, and the plant blooms over a long season while tolerating heat and drought once established. It draws butterflies and bees while in bloom and goldfinches to the seed heads later in the season. Deadhead to extend flowering, or leave the last flush of seed heads for winter bird forage, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Cherokee Sunset Rudbeckia (AAS-Winning Double Bronze-Gold Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Cherokee Sunset is an All-America Selections winner producing double and semi-double flowers in a warm mix of bronze, mahogany, and gold tones.

directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Cherokee Sunset is an All-America Selections winner bred from black-eyed Susan for unusually full, double and semi-double flowers in a rich mix of bronze, mahogany, rust, and gold tones, a striking departure from the single golden-yellow blooms of the straight species. It flowers heavily from summer through fall on sturdy, well-branched plants, providing long-lasting cut flowers and reliable garden color while tolerating Gulf South heat and drought once established. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the display going, and though it is usually grown as a warm-season annual or short-lived biennial, plants may self-seed and return in favorable spots.

common_name: Denver Daisy Rudbeckia (AAS-Winning Heat-Tolerant Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Denver Daisy is an All-America Selections winner bred for a compact, heat-tolerant habit and large gold flowers with a distinctive dark chocolate-brown center ring.

directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Denver Daisy is an All-America Selections winner producing large, clear golden-yellow flowers with a distinctive dark chocolate-brown ring encircling the central cone, on a compact, heat-tolerant plant that blooms heavily and continuously from early summer well into fall. Its sturdy, well-branched habit and strong performance in hot conditions make it a dependable choice for Gulf South borders and mass plantings, and it is highly attractive to bees and butterflies. Deadhead to extend flowering, and though usually grown as a warm-season annual or short-lived biennial, it self-seeds readily and often returns on its own in favorable spots.

common_name: Henry Eilers Rudbeckia (Quilled-Petal Native Sweet Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Henry Eilers was discovered growing wild in an Illinois prairie remnant and is prized for its distinctive quilled, tubular petals.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun. Henry Eilers, discovered growing wild in an Illinois prairie remnant and named for the naturalist who found it, is a striking selection of native sweet coneflower with golden-yellow petals rolled into distinctive narrow quills rather than the typical flat ray form, giving each flower a spidery, unusual look quite different from other Rudbeckia. The tall, sturdy, well-branched plant bears fragrant, anise-scented foliage and blooms heavily from late summer into fall, providing valuable late-season nectar for pollinators and seed for goldfinches. It tolerates average to moist soil better than many drought-loving Rudbeckia species, making it a good fit for a rain garden edge as well as a standard border. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
